It is a Persian word, on which see the material collected in Thes. vol. 1 p. 929. The verb derived from it, παρηγγάρευσε [he relayed the message], Bamberger restored at Ag. 289 in place of παραγγείλασα [having announced].

Thus Toupius Emend. vol. 3 p. 155 corrected with sufficient probability the corrupt reading in Antig. Cap. Hist. mir. c. 115 (127) p. 174 ed. Beckm. (88 ed. West.): ἄδων ταῖς ἁγναῖς παρθένοις γαμηλίων λέκτρων ἀστει μὴ βλεμμάτων ῥεπιβουλη (ῥέπει βολή [the glance inclines] Salmasius). With Toupius's conjecture should be compared what Antigonus brought from the same part of the Aeschylean play: νέας γυναικὸς — ἥτις ἀνδρὸς ἢ γεγευμένη [of a young woman — who has tasted of a man].
For downward to the pure maidens, inexperienced in marriage beds, the glance of their eyes inclines.
